title: Hundreds of layoffs and many cancelled projects later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reportedly says 'we will not survive' without new IPs
summary: Having one's cake and eating it too is meant to be a metaphor.
body: Thousands of layoffs , a couple of booted studios, and a re-organisation of Obsidian away from its newer projects and onto Fallout later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly taken to an internal town hall and talked about the importance of new IP. The transcript, as shared by Windows Central , goes as follows: "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive [sic] on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences." This is, to put it gently, very confusing. As part of Xbox's "Reset", the studio has done the following: Cancelled multiple projects from Obsidian and told it to go make a Fallout game . Made Double Fine go independent . Did the same to South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games . Put its sights on Arkane Lyon . Is, at present, in consultation talks regarding Ninja Theory after attempted sales failed. That doesn't smack to me of the kind of courage and new IP invention that Sharma is talking about—most of these studios had either just made in…

title: Planet Zoo 2 review: Superstar animals and frustrating micromanagement
summary: The animals are as beautiful as ever, but they're trapped in a cage of rote micromanagement.
body: Need to know What is it? Zoo-based management sim with added fish, birds, and nature reserves. Expect to Pay: $50/£40 Developer: Frontier Developments Publisher: Frontier Developments Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Nvidia 2080 Super, 32 GB RAM, Windows 10 Steam Deck: Verified Multiplayer: No, but you can share creations. Link: Official site Planet Zoo 2's animals are truly majestic creations. Even at a time when games are gnawing at the chain-link fence of photorealism, watching Frontier's meticulously modelled critters clamber and prowl, swim and fly, or play with whatever enrichment toys you've dunked into their enclosures, is always a treat. Like watching animals in a real zoo, there's a soothing, almost therapeutic quality to it. title: Museum strings together 30 old Mac minis for replica of most successful supercomputer, builds something more powerful than the original
summary: Happy birthday, Apple.
body: What's better than giving the hardware you already own a fresh lease on life ? Dedicating your older tech to resurrecting even older supercomputers. At least, that's if you ask the Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain . The hardware history museum recently used 30 Mac Minis dating between 2012 and 2014 to resurrect the Cray-1 supercomputer (via Ars Technica ). Debuting in the bygone year of 1976, the Cray-1 is noted for its striking C-shaped cabinet. However, what's arguably most impactful about the new display is that its composite parts make it technically more powerful than the original machine. The museum's exhibit features five quad-core i7s, and 25 dual-core i5s, resulting in a total of 70 cores to play with. The 30 Mac Minis run on Mojave, leveraging MacOS' Message Passing Interface to pass off computing tasks between them. When all of these cores were online during testing, the exhibit achieved 1.5 teraflops. The original Cray-1 had a 64-bit, 80 MHz processor and 8.39 MB of memory (PDF warning), with a theoretical peak performance of about 160 megaflops. It's a fitting tribute to both Apple and the Cray-1's 50th birthday this year. (Image credit: Museo de Historia …

title: I am the controller now: MIT engineers have created a 'second skin' that could one day track whole bodies in VR
summary: Riding the wave(guide).
body: Remember when they did motion capture on a cube ? Well, more specifically, they put actor Jack Quaid in a motion capture suit and then they put him inside a cube for his role in God of War Laufey. As charming as that cutting edge cuboid is, I think VR gamers and Vtubers are gonna be all over fresh research out of MIT. Engineers at MIT have developed a sheet full of optical fibres that can digitally reconstruct its own shape even as it is flexed and folded. According to MIT News , the team reckons their tech could be fashioned into a garment that could then be used to accurately mirror your real-world movements in a game. Though currently a bulky prototype, the flexible sheet could one day be worn like a second skin that can more accurately track the transformation of a surface, rather than the movement of, say, fixed points on a traditional motion capture suit. What's arguably even cooler though is that the sheet is shown in a demo video to remain functional even as an engineer pierces it with a hole puncher . title: The RTX 4090 launched four years ago today, and now the RTX 5090 is rumoured for the chop, I can't help but look upon it with a warm glow
summary: Times, they have a-changed.
body: Join me in saying "Happy birthday" to the RTX 4090, Nvidia's enthusiast-level graphics card of the previous generation. It launched four years ago today, October 12, with an eye-watering MSRP of $1,499. Well, eye-watering for the time. The cheapest RTX 5080 I can find right now is this Asus Prime variant for $1,640 , which is a sure sign of how things have changed in the past four years. When the second-from-top Nvidia card is now significantly more expensive than the launch MSRP of the previous generation big boi model, it's pretty easy to see how far we've fallen. And the RTX 4090's direct replacement, the RTX 5090, has reached near-unobtanium status. We've stopped tracking it on our graphics card price watch page , as the only listings around are priced at ludicrous levels from third-party sellers we're not comfortable recommending. Now rumours suggest Nvidia may have halted production of RTX 5090 chips for the consumer market , with the GB202 silicon being used for data center and professional GPUs instead. title: Here come the weird and wonderful mods for the Steam Frame, as Valve drops the full CAD files for free
summary: I bet someone is already mocking up cat ears for this thing.
body: Valve has released the CAD files for the Steam Frame , allowing modders the perfect opportunity to get to work on their own creations for the VR headset. The light blocker—the bit that sits between the bridge of your nose and the headset—is primed for user replacement, as are the head strap, battery housing, facial interface and more. This CAD release includes the lot, along with the core module and controllers. Valve has confirmed it is working on an upgraded head strap with interchangeable batteries and off-ear speakers for the Steam Frame. That's " coming soon ". With this CAD release, perhaps we'll see more options for third parties in future, too. The docs also detail how to interface with the expansion port , or auxiliary port as Valve calls it. This sits just to the front of the user's nose and is a way for a user to add in powered accessories, ie the Arcturus Vision RGB camera—I've been playing around with that for a couple of weeks and it's a pretty wicked upgrade. With one Gen4 PCIe lane alongside power and camera functionality, all laid out in the docs, there's a bunch more that could be done with the port. I'm just hoping someone runs with it. With this release, Valve …

title: Shogun 2 deserved better
summary: The visual upgrade is nice, but Complete Edition is a little lacking in QoL.
body: I blink and I've somehow spent another 30 hours in Shogun 2. Undoubtedly my favorite of the older Total War games—and I don't say that lightly as someone who also has big hour counts in Rome and Medieval 2—there's just something so straightforward about the second Shogun; an elegant simplicity complimented by a period where the Creative Assembly was clearly having fun experimenting with all sorts of ideas. It's no wonder it chose to remaster the game despite the fact it's arguably the best aged Total War there is. I'd happily go back and play Shogun 2 over Rome 2, or even Attila, which I think speaks to how well it holds up. It's definitely nice to play Shogun 2 with improved visuals (if you like the new style), modern unit controls, and full Japanese voice acting, but I think Creative Assembly missed the mark in terms of the remaster's other additions. To give it a fair shot, I started with one of the newly introduced island-bound minor factions, Honma. title: Steam Week in Review: The curious case of Wonder Boy in Monster Land's dubious PC debut
summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending October 11.
body: Wonder Boy in Monster Land released in Japanese arcades in 1987 and for the Sega Master System the following year. Its success led to numerous ports, including to ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari ST. Oddly, it never received an official PC port, though that long absence appeared to have come to an end on September 28. Did fans rejoice? Not really. The Steam listing for Wonderboy in Monster Land raises one immediate red flag: note the rookie error of "Wonderboy" versus Wonder Boy. The developer and publisher is Retro Maniac, whose only other Steam game is Street Hoop, or Street Slam, an old Data East arcade game from 1994. To bring you up to speed: LAT Corp owns all IP and assets once belonging to Westone Bit Entertainment, the creators of the original Wonder Boy games. But at the same time Sega, confusingly, owns the Wonder Boy trademark. In other words: LAT Corp owns the games, Sega owns the name. Both parties would need to OK any Wonder Boy re-release bearing the Wonder Boy name. Box art for Wonder Boy in Monster Land on Master System (Image credit: Sega) While the "Wonderboy" misspelling is damning, a Wonder Boy game appearing on Steam without SEGA or LAT Corp prominently di…

title: Star Wars Galactic Racer's devs tested its roguelite progression system by turning it into a board game
summary: "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system."
body: Years ago, I read that Jake Solomon prototyped the Firaxis reboot of XCOM by making a simple board game version. Something rudimentary that could be played in the office on scrap paper to get ideas across and figure out where the fun would be, without having to commit. But it's surprising to hear the same idea being used for a game as different from XCOM's turn-based tactics as Star Wars Galactic Racer. As Fuse Games' creative director Kieran Crimmins told Eurogamer , "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." And so the early prototype of this high-speed arcade racing game was indeed a board game. "You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software," CEO Matt Webster said, "but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment-to-moment." Specifically, the board game simulated Galactic Racer's progression system. Its rewards differ based on the event, but typically offer tuning points to spend on one of three random stats, and maybe a part for your speeder that …

title: Seamless Landing mod looks set to bring Starfield another step closer to No Man's Sky
summary: Or Star Wars Outlaws, if you're nasty.
body: There are mods for Seamless Grav Jumps and for Seamless Planet Takeoffs . But when you arrive at a planet in Starfield you still have to choose a landing spot, and then watch a loading screen and an animation. It's another thing that contributes to the feeling your spaceship is more like a house that can teleport. When you're in space, Starfield's planets are basically just textures you can fly right through if you put in the hours to try it, as Alanah Pearce discovered back when the RPG's boundaries were still being explored. It seemed like one gap modders would never be able to paper over, but Frederik Wessberg has apparently managed it. The video of his work-in-progress mod shows a planetary approach, complete with heating effects on the ship during atmospheric entry, a moment of white as he hits a layer of clouds, and then the ship just lands. It seems like the clouds are there to mask a moment of loading, but Wessberg says "the cloud cover is in fact not a fancy loading screen." title: Yahtzee is still out there being mean about videogames, and good for him
summary: Zero Punctuation was an essential watch back in the day. Its successor Fully Ramblomatic still carries the torch.
body: When the HMS Escapist sank everyone worth a damn swam away to form a YouTube channel called Second Wind , where Yahtzee Croshaw's video series Zero Punctuation continued under the name Fully Ramblomatic. It's not exactly the same—the people have glasses now—but it's continuing the essential work of being rude about videogames on the internet. Back in the Before Times, when someone brought a videogame magazine to school we'd all gather round to flick through it, and the only measure of whether it was a good videogame magazine was if the captions on the screenshots were funny. I didn't notice until years later, but that meant we only read the British ones. That particularly British tone is something Yahtzee's videos share. It might come across as flippant to some, but to me it's always read as deep care. Putting in the effort to make a description witty instead of plain means you're working harder to keep your audience engaged, and doing that for videogames suggests you care enough about them to want your audience to actually pay attention. Yahtzee does that. Like Blackadder finding the 100th way to tell Baldrick he's an idiot, he never runs out of ways to complain about videogames.…

title: Nier creator Yoko Taro says he's achieved his career dreams, but he continues working because it's 'good for preventing dementia'
summary: "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted."
body: They say that art is never finished, only abandoned—but that doesn't seem to be the case for Yoko Taro, creator of Nier and Drakengard, who you might recognize by the round, smiley Emil mask he wears. According to a report from Denfaminicogamer (via IGN ), Taro said at the Tokyo French Institute last month that he's already more or less realized his vision and has considered retiring. "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted," Taro said. "As a game otaku, I think the dream is to release something you've always wanted to create into the world. Having achieved that dream, I view everything after that as the remainder of my life." As for why he continues to work in gamedev if he's already achieved his dreams, well, he said the money doesn't hurt—and that he has a fear of how his mental health might degrade should he grow idle. "This is good for preventing dementia," he said. It's worth noting that Taro is, to put it in technical terms, a bit of a silly goose, if the mask didn't tip you off. title: RPGs are simply better when you're an idiot
summary: I just can't relate to these capable heroes.
body: Dungeon Master (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke. Most videogame RPGs are selling a power fantasy—the idea that you are competent, clever and regardless of the odds will still manage to save the day. Fate has made you a hero, and nothing is going to stop you from achieving your goals. And this holds a lot of appeal. It's sometimes nice to be able to take a holiday from my own incompetence. Over the last few days I've managed to drop my dinner, get trapped on a bus going in the wrong direction, get peed on by a dog, get almost run over by a car and, to top it all off, actually get knocked over by an electric scooter. I am a walking disaster. (Image credit: BioWare) Geralt never gets peed on. Shepard never lands on their arse after colliding with a teen. These are not heroic moments. When these protagonists face adversity, it only serves as an excuse for more badass adventures. It turns out, though, that constantly winning becomes a little dull. I want more friction. So I've found a happy medium, playing a strategy roguelike that provides players with "all the satisfaction of reaching rank 1, none of the toxic teammates or 40-minute hostage games". title: This Control-inspired action game set in a 'planet-scale alien mind' has one of the most stunning art styles I've seen this year
summary: Studio Lifeforms' Etre is shaping up to be a visual feast.
body: In the age of near photorealism, it takes a lot for a game's visuals to impress me. As cramming yet more pixels into a videogame character's face provides diminishing returns, standing out from the crowd is increasingly about how creative developers get in applying that power. All that said, I was genuinely mesmerised by the debut footage of Etre , an upcoming action adventure game with a truly eye-popping art style. Created by LA-based developer Studio Lifeforms, Etre is a narrative driven-action game set on Orbis, which Studio Lifeforms describes as a "planet-scale alien mind on the brink of awakening". You play as a character named Xyle, who arrives at this sentient cityscape in search of his soulmate Atel. According to Studio Lifeforms, the game's distinctive visuals are inspired by graphic novels of the '70s and '80s. Studio Lifeforms doesn't specify which graphics novels, and I am too much of a comics philistine to tell you. But the result is an incredibly distinctive visual style. In terms of games, Etre's closest visual cousins are the likes of Rez and Tetris Effect . But Etre applies its aesthetics to a much more grounded type of game. From a mechanical perspective, Studi…

title: Deadlock's City Never Sleeps update makes Valve's MOBA my favorite videogame setting in years
summary: I wanna be a part of it, New York, New York.
body: Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. I've plenty of glowing words for Deadlock, but its latest update, City Never Sleeps, is like seeing one of the last few hammer-blows of a masterpiece. title: Deadlock surpasses Team Fortress 2's all-time concurrent player count peak as it adds a chess wizard
summary: Siri, call my pawns.
body: Valve's latest MOBA might still technically be conducting an invite-only test, but it's nevertheless one of the most popular games of its ilk. Yesterday, right as the game added the latest in its current batch of six new democratically released heroes , its concurrent player-count hit a new screaming high: 262,145 simultaneous players, according to SteamDB . While that's pretty impressive on its face, it'll be especially noteworthy to long-time fans of Valve's games that this surge of activity brought Deadlock past Team Fortress 2's all-time concurrent player count peak of 253,997. Though this doesn't include the player numbers TF2 saw on the Xbox 360 and PS3 as part of The Orange Box, which I'm sure were positively through the roof, it's still conceivably its genuine peak given that it was just three years ago. As for how TF2's history of botting issues and idle servers might have affected that number, I can't say. It's not a one-to-one—PC gaming was a smaller phenomenon overall when TF2 was at the height of its popularity, and its Quake-descended slapstick arguably appeals to a smaller crowd than a hero shooter-MOBA hybrid does today—but it's an impressive showing for Deadlock g…

title: The studio behind Star Wars Zero Company is bringing back some of its furloughed staff
summary: "[The furlough] was an incredibly difficult decision, but one that was necessary to help us eventually bring back as many people as possible."
body: Just as Star Wars Zero Company was set to launch earlier this year, developer Bit Reactor furloughed over 80% of its staff over sales uncertainty . In other words, much of its staff were receiving no pay, despite technically being employees, right when players were getting their hands on the game. Earlier this week on Bluesky , the studio announced it had begun undoing this "difficult decision" (via gamesindustry.biz ). Bit Reactor CEO Greg Foertsch said in the statement that the decision was made in response to "unexpected business developments outside of our control," but that it was "necessary to help us eventually bring as many people back as possible." According to Game File , an unnamed source "familiar with the situation" has said that the developer's payroll is back up to more than half what it was before the furloughs. When this first happened, Game File reported that 80 percent of Bit Reactor employees were affected, hamstringing any sort of support following the game's release, and that the decision fell with Bit Reactor, not publisher EA. title: Be warned: Nivalis Nights may not be the cozy game you expect: 'If you want a cozy existence in this city, you're going to have to earn it'
summary: It wouldn't be the first cozy game with horrific debts to pay, though.
body: The popular user-added tags for Nivalis Nights on Steam are: Cyberpunk, simulation, life sim, management, and relaxing. It is definitely a cyberpunk shop/life sim, but relaxing? This one was on the wishlists of a lot of cozy gaming fans, including me. After playing it though, I'm not sure it's the kind of cozy most people would expect. Here's what lead writer Thomas Welsh had to say: The volume of quests and story content in Nivalis Nights feels overwhelming at times. Was that intentional? The cozy is right there, on the rich people island, nearly obscured by my stuffed quest HUD. (Image credit: Ion Lands) Well, cozy always has been in the eye of the beholder

title: The advent of first-person shooters introduced a wild frontier of unregulated video game level packs, and it ended in a lawsuit that changed copyright forever
summary: Revisiting the forgotten fourth state of PC gaming.
body: Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager . For most of PC gaming history, there were three states of PC game—your regular old video game, expansions/DLC, and mods. But for a brief period in the 1990s, there was a fourth state, the level pack—collections of levels for the early first-person shooters like Duke Nukem 3D and Quake . These level packs were sold on shelves as boxed products just like their video game counterparts. But they occupied a far more amorphous position between the other three states of PC gaming. In form and structure, they were similar to expansions, and are sometimes bundled into the same category. The Master Levels for Doom 2, for example, are regarded as an official expansion to that game. Others, however, were marketed as "Official Mission Packs," like Quake's additional episodes Scourge of Armagon and Dissolution of Eternity. On top of …

title: Expect plenty more Silent Hill over the next few years, as Konami has plans for 'second and third waves' of new games in its revived horror series
summary: "We're currently looking at a number of projects," says producer Motoi Okamoto.
body: Silent Hill's resurrection is one of the happier stories to emerge from the games industry in recent years. After spending roughly a decade locked in a Konami cupboard, Silent Hill has received three new entries published by Konami in as many years, all of which arrived to positive reviews and, seemingly, healthy sales. But if Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f , and Silent Hill: Townfall still haven't satisfied your craving for allegorical horror in foggy towns, fret not, because Konami has plenty more plans for the series' ongoing revival. In an interview featured in Famitsu (via IGN ), Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto explained that Konami is "relieved" by both the critical and commercial reception to the aforementioned three games. "All three titles we initially announced were able to be released successfully," Okamoto said, adding that, "they've also received high praise, and we are satisfied with it." Okamoto went on to say that the games released so far only represent the "first wave" of Konami's planned games for the series, and that there's not one but two additional waves on the drawing board.
